To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of raw historical project data as a calibration set for estimation models may be misleading, and (2) the use of historical data as the “ground truth” for evaluating the accuracy of (any) estimation model is problematic.
(1) historical project data is an unreliable source for estimating project duration, and (2) historical project data should not be used for calibrating or evaluating (new) software estimation models.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the use of raw historical project data for the purpose of calibrating and validating software estimation tools is a valid and useful practice.

the utility of historical data for estimating future projects, and we conclude that the current research practices in the software estimation field may be flawed in this respect.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
raw historical project data is neither the best nor worst source of data for estimating future projects.
the current practice of using raw project statistics for calibration and evaluation is not only insufficient but also misleading.
the utility of historical data for estimation is highly dependent upon the specific nature of the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although historical project statistics are a necessary input for any (new) estimation tool, they are not sufficient.
the use of raw historical project data as a benchmark for estimating future software development projects may be misleading.
the utility of historical projects statistics for calibrations and evaluations of estimation tools is highly questionable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way in which estimation tools are currently evaluated and calibrated is not ideal.

the industry needs to be more careful about how it uses historical project data in the calibration and evaluation of new cost and duration estimation models, and that it should be less dependent on such data for future estimation.
it is imperative to understand and account for the underlying process dynamics when evaluating the accuracy and utility of (new) project estimation tools.
